executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the United States' aggressive repositioning toward its adversaries and neighbors in the Western Hemisphere and beyond, with the Trump administration driving a series of confrontational moves that carry significant geopolitical consequence. The New York Times reports U.S. charges against Raúl Castro, while The Economist details Trump's push toward an endgame in Cuba — together signaling a sharp escalation of pressure on Havana that breaks from decades of cautious engagement. The Economist's newsletter further argues that Trump's broader policy agenda amounts to a self-imposed 'MAGA tax' constraining American economic competitiveness, suggesting these foreign policy gambits come at a domestic cost. Foreign Affairs deepens the stakes by framing Iran through a Vietnam lens and analyzing how China and Russia stand to exploit American overextension, while also diagnosing why Mexico's cartels remain structurally resistant to U.S. pressure — a reminder that muscular posturing rarely translates into durable strategic wins. Taken together, today's content makes a clear case that Washington is placing multiple high-stakes bets simultaneously, with allies, adversaries, and markets all watching whether resolve will produce results or accelerate vulnerabilities.

newsletters.title: 🔴 The Insider: The MAGA tax is holding America back

items.headline: The MAGA tax is holding America back
items.blurb: For the past year America has been running a giant experiment. What happens when you take one of the world's most successful economies and put in place two big growth-busting changes: tariffs and a sudden stop in immigration? Many observers—including us—thought the impact would be unambiguously negative. Yet America's economy is still the envy of the rich world. The country's GDP grew faster than that of any other G7 country last year. Its stockmarkets have repeatedly hit record highs over the past 15 months. What is going on? We have crunched the numbers. An artificial-intelligence boom, soaring stockmarkets and some of Donald Trump's own measures have boosted the economy. But by our calculations, the president's chaotic policymaking, sweeping tariffs and mass deportations are, in fact, hurting growth—a drag we call the "MAGA tax". Our calculations suggest that without the MAGA tax, America's economy would have grown more than half a percentage point faster.
